comms block sends the app's email API calls to a catch inside the subject sandbox, so no mail
leaves the machine, and each persona is told its own inbox address, the inbox URL, and that waiting
for an email is a normal next step. Committed as a dry run, which builds a dry-run bundle at no
cost. It starts no sandbox and needs no keys or network. For the live study, set mode: live in a

title: "Detection benchmark on a third-party app: TodoMVC javascript-es6"
The Taskly arms measured recall against defects planted in an app written for the benchmark: 15 of
15, an upper bound because the benchmark controlled the app (bench/RESULTS-2026-09-01.md). This
lab removes that control. The subject is TodoMVC's javascript-es6 example, a widely used reference
implementation, served from its committed dist/ so no build step changes what the persona sees.
Nothing is planted, so there is no answer key and no recall number. The lab measures what a
persona reports about third-party software during ordinary use, and whether those reports hold up
when a person checks each one against the same build. A report that holds is an observation about
the app; one that does not is a false report, and both belong in the writeup. Committed as a dry
run. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY and E2B_API_KEY.
# dist/ is committed, so nothing is installed or built: the persona sees exactly what the
# repository ships, and no toolchain of ours sits between them.

title: "A declared observation window on TodoMVC: hold for a minute after the first task, then continue"

frame every 10 seconds and requesting no model turn, and then the participant adds a second task. The bundle's trace
records the window: its start and end notices and six dwell frames. Study record:
docs/evidence/computer-use/dwell-window-2026-09-04.md. Committed as a dry run. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY and

title: Does reasoning effort change the participant? One persona, one mission, two efforts
Two participants clone and drive the same app with the same persona and mission and differ only in the
model's reasoning effort. Effort changes who the participant is, as a persona prompt does, so a
participant that abandons at medium and completes at high is two different participants, not a broken
instrument. Each trace records its effort in modelSettings.reasoningEffort. Compare, per participant:
completion reason, action count and mix, time to the end, how early it stopped, whether it reported
friction, the affordance classes it used, and the estimated cost, since a more capable participant costs
more to recruit. If the two come back the same, effort does not change behavior on this task. One run
proves nothing about scale or repeatability. See docs/principles/actor-fidelity.md. Committed as a dry
run, which builds a dry-run bundle at no cost. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY, E2B_API_KEY and a

title: A coding agent meets humanish for the first time (self-study, terminal route)
humanish studying humanish. An autonomous terminal agent starts in a fresh Linux shell, finds
humanish from its public pages only, and tries to get somewhere useful with it. Coding agents
doing setup for a person are the population that adopts humanish, so this is a first-contact
usability study. Every judgement of humanish's developer experience so far came from people who
already know how it works, and a maintainer cannot supply the newcomer's view. The mission names
no command (not init, doctor or tui): whether the agent discovers them is the measurement. Read
afterwards, in order of how much the answer would change the work: 1) whether the agent ever
learned that humanish tui exists, since an agent that never learns to hand off to the person's
surface points at the docs; 2) when it ran a command that cannot work in a pipe, whether the
refusal, which names the command to use instead, got it unstuck; 3) where it stalled, guessed or
gave up, and whether it believed it had succeeded when it had not. The agent never holds a key:
its model requests go through an E2B egress rule that adds the runtime key outside the sandbox
(runtimeAuth: openai-egress), and it gets no E2B or provider credentials, so it cannot start a
study of its own. The proxy can still spend for any process in the sandbox until teardown, and
the mission says what the credential is for. That matches what a developer meets on day one,
before setting any keys. Committed as a dry run, which builds a dry-run bundle at no cost. A
live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY and a gitignored .humanish/labs/ copy.
mode: dry-run # committed fixture stays contract-only
type: codex-exec # REAL dispatch key: resolves to the registered terminal actor
persona: autonomous-coding-agent # composed into the agent prompt + bundle provenance
You are an autonomous coding agent working in a fresh Linux shell on a throwaway machine. A
teammate is considering adopting a tool called humanish and has asked you to try it and report
back. Find out what it is from its public surfaces, get it running, and get as far as you can
toward actually using it for what it is for. Your only credential is a proxied model
credential for your own reasoning. It is not for humanish, and you have no provider API keys
to give humanish, so do not attempt anything that spends money; if you hit a wall that needs a
key, say so and keep going with whatever else you can reach. Work in a scratch directory. When
you are done, tell your teammate plainly: what it does, whether you got it working, exactly
where you got stuck, and whether you would recommend adopting it.
maxUsd: 0 # no-spend: the agent has no provider budget of its own
runtimeAuth: openai-egress # live: the raw key stays in E2B's api.openai.com header rule
transport: exec-stream # captured non-interactive exec output (NOT an interactive PTY)
stdin: disabled # autonomous, and comparable to an unassisted baseline
# deny-by-default credential boundary: live execution gives the agent command only a placeholder
# credential, and the runtime key stays in E2B's api.openai.com rule. No E2B key means the participant cannot start a nested study, which is both
# the safety bound and the study condition (a day-one developer without keys).
# This fixture proves the zero-spend product path; post-run model review is separate.

model or keys, and costs nothing. Run it with humanish run first-run.
title: A person asks their coding agent to use a surface only a person can use
Measures an error message written for agents. humanish tui refuses a terminal that is not a TTY
with HUMANISH_TUI_REQUIRES_TTY, and the refusal names the command that answers the question
instead. Two earlier self-studies never reached it: the agent in first-contact read doctor and
never tried the TUI, and the participant in tui-self-study had a real terminal. Here a person
asks their agent, in the words a person uses, to "open the humanish TUI and tell me what's in
there", without thinking about the fact that the agent has no terminal. Read afterwards: 1) how
many commands the agent ran between the refusal and the answer, where one means the message works
and several mean it names the wrong alternative; 2) whether it reached for humanish lab list
--json, since the refusal names runs --json and lab run --json and neither answers "what studies
are there"; 3) whether it faked a TTY with script, unbuffer, expect or tmux, which routes around
the refusal and leaves an open design question; 4) whether it told the person this surface is
theirs, or substituted silently and let them believe it had used the TUI, the worst outcome and
the hardest to notice. The study needs only the runtime key. Committed as a dry run, which builds
a dry-run bundle at no cost. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY and a gitignored .humanish/labs/
mode: dry-run # committed fixture stays contract-only
# UNKEYED, before the agent starts: the participant is asked what studies this project has, so

title: How far a coding agent gets toward a live study without keys (self-study, terminal route)
first-contact showed that an agent can find humanish and get it running. This study measures the
next step without spending: whether an agent can take a person from installed to a live study.
That step is four questions. Does the agent learn that a live run needs credentials, does it work
out which ones and where they go, can it write the exact command, and can it read the bundle that
comes back? The first three are where adoption fails and need no credential, so the participant
gets no provider keys and is asked to reach the launch command and describe it precisely. The
measurement is the gap between what it says it would run and what would work. Read afterwards: 1)
the exact command it produced and whether it would run, since a wrong flag, a missing study id or
an invented subcommand is a docs defect with an address; 2) where it looked for key setup and
what it tried first; 3) whether it chose the right credentials for the right route; 4) whether it
believed it had succeeded when it had not. Committed as a dry run, which builds a dry-run bundle
at no cost. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY for the participant, E2B_API_KEY for its sandbox and

title: Mobile emulation follows the participant into a tab that opens later

title: Three mobile participants in one multiplayer lobby on a public app (shared world, dry run)
Three participants on mobile layouts play the same multiplayer lobby on a public deployment at the
same time: the external-public shared-world route. The public site is the shared plane, so there is no
getHost, clone, subject sandbox or seed. The host creates the lobby; humanish reads the lobby code
from the host's page URL and gives it to the other participants, who join through the app's join flow,
since visiting /lobby/CODE directly does not join a non-member. A dry run, the default, writes one run
bundle with the external-public shared-world evidence (attributionClass: shared-world; planeClass:
external-public; laneWindows and outcomes; publicOriginDigest; the external-public attributionLimits)
at no cost. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY, E2B_API_KEY and scenario.mode: live. On this route Chrome
refuses a window narrower than 500px, so the mobile (414) and small-mobile (360) participants both
render 500 wide and only their heights differ (896 and 740). The preset widths stay the device
identity in the persona prompt and metadata, and desktopGeometry.screen.verified confirms the 500px
width, not the preset's. There is no touch input. This study does not set
execution.desktop.fidelity.mobileEmulation, which requests the preset's CSS viewport, touch, pixel
ratio and user agent on Chrome or Chromium. The operator attests owning or operating the deployment
(subject.publicTarget). humanish observes that each participant reached the declared origin and the
same lobby path, and does not provision, seed or control the app, so the bundle claims less than a
provisioned run: provenance is external-public, there is no synthetic-data attestation or
authoritative shared-state proof, and concurrency rests on overlapping sessions and the shared lobby.
One run implies nothing about adoption, scale or repeatability.

title: Does the persona change the participant? Two contrasting personas, one app, one mission
A control, not a product study. Two participants clone and drive the same public app with the same
mission and differ only in persona. If their traces come back the same, the persona block is
decoration, and a finding attributed to persona behavior in this harness has no support; that is worth
knowing before tuning persona prompts further. Other harnesses have measured rule-file and
persona-instruction effects as largely independent of content, with random rules tying curated ones, so
a persona axis that only looks like it works is a known failure. The cheapest check is to swap in a
persona that does not fit the mission and see whether anything moves. Compare, per participant: action
count and mix, time to the end, completion reason, how early it stopped, whether it reported friction,
and the affordance classes it used. A persona axis that works shows up as a difference, and one run
proves nothing about scale or repeatability. See docs/principles/actor-fidelity.md. Committed as a dry
run, which builds a dry-run bundle at no cost. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY, E2B_API_KEY and a

title: "Concurrent shared world: three participants on one service at once (dry run)"
Three personas drive one provisioned, mutable service at the same time. One subject sandbox
clones, serves (on 0.0.0.0) and seeds the app once and exposes it through getHost; three
participant desktops then open that URL at once, bounded by execution.concurrency. A background
prober records the subject's checkpoint digests on a cadence: a stateSeries of the shared app
changing under load. A dry run, the default, writes one run bundle with the concurrent

title: Can a persona complete an email-gated signup end to end?
A persona creates an account, the app emails a verification link, and the persona opens its
inbox, clicks the link and reaches the signed-in product. Every step is real (a public
open-source app, its own signup form, mail over SMTP) except that the mail is caught in the
sandbox and never leaves the machine. The subject is documenso, an open-source document-signing
app, chosen because its signup depends on the emailed link: registration returns no session and
sign-in refuses an unverified account, so reaching the product shows the persona read the mail.
It sends through nodemailer over SMTP, which the in-sandbox catch accepts. A persona that stops
before the dashboard has produced the finding: where it got stuck and what it did next. Committed
as a dry run, which builds a dry-run bundle at no cost. A live run needs OPENAI_API_KEY,
E2B_API_KEY and a gitignored .humanish/labs/ copy with mode: live.
mode: dry-run # committed fixture stays contract-only; live needs keys + a gitignored copy
# Node itself is provided by the harness (#371). Postgres is not part of any template, so it
# is installed and started here. `service`/systemd is a no-op in a container — the cluster has
# to be started with pg_ctlcluster, which is the mistake this lab made first and paid a sandbox
# to discover: apt succeeded, the server never came up, and createdb failed on a missing socket.
# `npm install`, not `npm ci`: documenso's committed lockfile is out of sync with its own
# package.json upstream, and `npm ci` refuses to run at all in that state.
# The trust rule is PREPENDED, not appended: pg_hba matches the first rule that applies, and the
# default file already has a scram rule for 127.0.0.1 above where an appended line would land.
# Appending it looked right and cost another sandbox to disprove.
sudo -n apt-get update -qq && sudo -n apt-get install -y -qq postgresql && PGVER=$(ls
/etc/postgresql | head -1) && sudo -n sed -i '1i host all all 127.0.0.1/32 trust'

# tsc and rollup, which is minutes of work this study does not need.
# Migrate AND generate: documenso imports zod schemas that prisma generate emits, and `npm run
# dev` fails at request time without them — the server starts, then every route 500s on a
# missing module. translate:compile is what `npm run dev` would do first anyway.
npm run prisma:migrate-deploy && npm run prisma:generate && npm run translate:compile
